title: S3 Security: Access Control, Encryption & Object Lock
summary: Bucket policies, Block Public Access, Object Ownership, encryption options and WORM retention for S3.
tldr: **Bucket policies** with condition keys do most of the work: `aws:SecureTransport` (HTTPS only), `aws:PrincipalOrgID` / `aws:PrincipalOrgPaths` (whole org or OU), `aws:SourceVpce` (one VPC endpoint only).

**Block Public Access** at the account level (protected by an SCP) is the guard that stops anything becoming public. **Object Ownership: bucket owner enforced** disables ACLs and makes the bucket owner own every object.

Encryption at rest: **SSE-S3** is automatic; pick **SSE-KMS** with a customer managed key when key use must be audited in CloudTrail and governed by a key policy, and add **S3 Bucket Keys** to cut KMS cost.
**Object Lock compliance mode** is true WORM: nobody, not even root, can delete objects or shorten retention. **Governance mode** can be bypassed by users with a special permission.

keyFacts.text: Since 5 January 2023 every new object is encrypted at rest with SSE-S3 automatically, at no cost. Default encryption doesn't touch objects that already existed.
New buckets have all four **Block Public Access** settings on and **ACLs disabled** (bucket owner enforced). Turning either off needs an explicit extra permission.
Since April 2026 new buckets block **SSE-C** uploads by default; a bucket must opt back in. Older questions may still offer SSE-C for customer-supplied keys.
Maximum bucket policy size. When many apps need different prefix rules, delegate to **S3 access points**, each with its own policy and optional VPC-only origin.
Object Lock needs **S3 Versioning** (turning Object Lock on enables it). Locks apply per object version; a bucket can set a default retention, and **legal holds** never expire on their own.
Cross-account reads of SSE-KMS objects need S3 permission **and** `kms:Decrypt` allowed in both the key policy and the caller's IAM policy.

traps: Governance mode plus an SCP is not regulatory WORM; the root user and bypass permission can still remove protection.
A legal hold has no end date and anyone with `s3:PutObjectLegalHold` can lift it, so it doesn't satisfy a fixed 7-year rule.
MFA Delete and lifecycle transitions don't stop a privileged user from deleting data.
Default encryption with SSE-KMS doesn't enforce HTTPS; encryption in transit needs `aws:SecureTransport`.
Traffic through a VPC endpoint uses private IPs, so `aws:SourceIp` can't pin access to it. Use `aws:SourceVpce`.
Turning on Block Public Access in each account isn't enough if admins can turn it off; add an SCP.
Using ACLs to fix cross-account object ownership is the legacy approach. Prefer bucket owner enforced.
Sharing a bucket through AWS RAM or listing every account ID is the high-overhead answer for org-wide access; use `aws:PrincipalOrgID`.
